candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on Luke
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXXVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

'This poor widow hath cast in more than they all' — Cyril reads the widow's mite as the canonical anchor of the all-or-nothing form of Christian almsgiving: the gift is measured not by the amount given but by the proportion of one's substance, and the widow who gives her last two coins gives literally everything. Tewahedo monastic voluntary poverty draws on Lk 21:3-4 as one of its earliest canonical anchors of total renunciation.

candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXXVII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Heb 10.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's prophecy 'there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down' (Lk 21:6), Cyril reads the Temple-destruction prophecy as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the canonical-end-of-the-Old-Covenant-cultus: the Temple as the chosen-place (Deu 12:5) is replaced by the eucharistic-altar in every local church. The destruction in 70 AD is the historical confirmation, but the spiritual transition is already accomplished in Christ. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Lk 21:6 + Heb 10 (sacrificial-system fulfilled in Christ's one offering) as the canonical doubled-witness for the New-Covenant transition; the tabot bearing the Christic-presence replaces the Temple as the dwelling of God.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'when ye shall hear of wars and commotions, be not terrified... the end is not by and by' (Lk 21:9), Cyril reads the not-by-and-by (ouk eutheōs — 'not immediately') qualification as the canonical Lukan anchor against eschatological-panic: military-and-political upheaval does NOT mean the end is now. Cyril notes the eschatological discourses regularly correct panic — Christian eschatology is patient, not feverish. Tewahedo eschatological-spirituality cites Lk 21:9 + 2 Th 2:1-2 (Pauline corrective against 'the day of the Lord is at hand' panic) as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of patient-eschatological-hope rather than panic-eschatology.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's promise 'I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist' (Lk 21:15), Cyril reads the doubled-gift (mouth-and-wisdom) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the Spirit's-utterance-in-persecution: when the disciple is delivered up before kings, the Spirit speaks IN him. The doctrine flows into Stephen's defense before the Sanhedrin (Acts 6:10 — 'they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake'). Tewahedo confessor-theology cites Lk 21:15 + Acts 6:10 as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of the Spirit-given confessor's-utterance; the Tewahedo martyrs (e.g. Ethiopian Christians under Imperial persecution) participate in this canonical promise.

On Christ's 'But there shall not an hair of your head perish' (Lk 21:18), Cyril reads the hyperbolic-hair-promise in juxtaposition with the immediately-preceding 'some of you shall they cause to be put to death' (21:16) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the spiritual-preservation-through-bodily-death: the believer who dies for Christ does not perish (the hair-of-the-head is not lost) — the apparent perishing is preserved-life in the heavenly economy. Tewahedo martyr-theology cites Lk 21:18 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of resurrection-preservation: every hair of the Tewahedo martyrs (Saint Yared, the Nine Saints, Imperial-era confessors) is preserved with God.

On Christ's 'Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled' (Lk 21:24), Cyril reads the times-of-the-Gentiles (kairoi ethnōn) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the Gentile-inclusion-interval: between the canonical-rejection of Christ at Calvary and the eschatological-restoration there is an apostolic-missionary period during which the Gentile-Ethiopian-nations are brought into the fold. Tewahedo missionary-eschatology cites Lk 21:24 + Rom 11:25 ('blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in') as the canonical Lukan-Pauline doubled-witness for the doctrine of the Tewahedo-Gentile-times — the Tewahedo Church's mission contributes to the fulfilment of the times of the Gentiles.

On Christ's 'when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh' (Lk 21:28), Cyril reads the doubled-imperative (look-up + lift-up-your-heads) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of upward-eschatological-orientation: the Christian's posture in eschatological-troubled-times is not downcast fear but upward-confident expectation. The redemption (apolytrōsis) draws-near is in present-tense participial form — the deliverance is approaching, not merely imminent. Tewahedo liturgical-posture cites Lk 21:28 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of standing-with-uplifted-eyes during the Eucharistic anaphora — the liturgical-posture embodies the eschatological-anticipation.

candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'Watch ye therefore, and pray always, that ye may be accounted worthy to escape all these things that shall come to pass, and to stand before the Son of man' (Lk 21:36), Cyril reads the watch-and-pray-always + stand-before-the-Son-of-Man as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of eschatological-vigilance grounded in ceaseless-prayer (doubled with Lk 18:1 — 'always to pray, and not to faint'). The stand-before-the-Son-of-Man is the canonical Lukan formula for eschatological-judgment-readiness. Tewahedo monastic-vigil-prayer (the night-office tradition of the great monasteries) cites Lk 21:36 + Lk 18:1 as the canonical doubled-Lukan-anchor for the ceaseless-prayer + eschatological-vigilance discipline.
